title: How to Triage the Compliance Inbox with Outlook Mail and Jinba
summary: Stop manually reading every compliance email to decide who owns it. This Jinba workflow classifies KYC requests, regulatory notices, and escalations automatically, with full audit logging.
body_markdown:
### Summary


- Compliance triage is a sorting function, not an investigation; the workflow handles classification, extraction, routing, and logging before a human makes the judgment call.
- The four-step flow triggers on a shared Outlook mailbox, classifies and extracts via Azure OpenAI or Anthropic, routes to the right team, and logs every decision to a Google Sheet.
- Classifications with confidence below 0.85 go to manual review instead of automatic routing.
- Key safeguards include reply-loop filtering, Microsoft Graph rate-limit handling, and keeping email data and AI inference inside the organization's own tenant.
- Map the top three to five recurring categories and run in observation mode for two to four weeks before enabling routing; build the workflow in[Jinba Flow](https://flow.jinba.io/) .


Compliance and operations teams typically manage a shared mailbox that receives KYC requests, regulatory notices, and internal escalations in the same stream, with no systematic way to separate them. The bottleneck is the manual effort of reading each message, determining what it needs, pulling out the relevant details, and deciding who should handle it, rather than the volume of email. That context-gathering work happens before any real compliance judgment is made and consumes the capacity that should go toward investigation and response.


This guide covers a four-step automated triage workflow built on Jinba: a trigger on incoming mail to a shared Outlook mailbox, an AI classification step using Azure OpenAI or Anthropic, a structured extraction of key fields, and a routing step that assigns the request and logs it to a case tracker. No external email is sent without human approval at any point in the workflow.


The four steps at a glance:


1. **Trigger:** A new email arrives in a shared Outlook mailbox.
2. **Classify:** An AI model categorizes the email as a KYC Request, Regulatory Notice, Internal Escalation, or General Inquiry.
3. **Extract:** Key fields are pulled from the email body: customer name, request type, deadline, and reference number.
4. **Route:** The request is assigned to the correct team and logged to a Google Sheet case tracker.


## Triage is a sorting function, not an investigation


Before building any automation, the process it supports needs to be clearly defined.[Effective compliance triage](https://www.ethico.com/insights/compliance-case-triage-framework-how-to-prioritize-investigations-when-every-report-feels-urgent-2) is a sorting function. Its job is to determine severity, assign priority, and route to the right owner. It is not the investigation itself.


This distinction matters for automation design. The workflow described here makes no compliance decisions. It reads, classifies, extracts, and routes. The investigator who receives the routed task makes the judgment call.


Two criteria govern effective triage:


- **Severity:** The potential regulatory or legal exposure if the request is not handled correctly.
- Urgency: Whether a regulatory response window or other hard deadline applies.


Automation applies these criteria consistently to every incoming message. It removes the variability that comes from different analysts applying different mental frameworks to the same inbox. Every email goes through the same logic, and every decision is recorded. That consistency is the foundation of a defensible audit trail.


## Step 1: Trigger on incoming email to a shared Outlook mailbox


The workflow begins when an email arrives at a centralized shared mailbox such ascompliance@yourcompany.com . A shared mailbox is the correct architecture here. Personal mailboxes fragment the intake process and make it impossible to apply a consistent triage rule across the team.


Jinba's[Outlook Mail tool](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/communication/outlook_mail) connects to the mailbox via the Microsoft Graph API, providing a secure and audited integration point. The` OUTLOOK_LIST_MESSAGES` action is a polling tool with no event trigger, so the workflow runs on a schedule: on each run, Jinba lists the messages in the shared mailbox and processes any new arrivals since the last run. This removes the need for manual checking and ensures the triage process begins without someone watching the inbox.


The listing step captures each raw message: sender, subject, body, and timestamp. These become the inputs for the classification step.


## Step 2: Classify email intent with Azure OpenAI or Anthropic


Subject lines in compliance inboxes are often vague. A message headed "Follow-up" or "Urgent" gives no indication of whether it requires a KYC response, a legal review, or a routing decision to a senior investigator. Analysts currently read each email in full to make that determination. This step automates that reading.


Jinba integrates with both[Azure OpenAI](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/ai/azure_openai) and[Anthropic](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/ai/anthropic) . Either model receives the email body and returns a structured classification. The prompt for this step is shown below:


You are a compliance triage assistant. Read the following email and classify it into exactly one of these categories:


- KYC Request
- Regulatory Notice
- Internal Escalation
- General Inquiry


Also return a confidence score between 0 and 1.


Respond in JSON with the fields: category, confidence.


Email:
{email_body}


The confidence score is critical.[Microsoft's technical guidance on AI email agents](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5933595/ai-email-agent-autonomous-email-monitoring-classif) identifies the handling of low-confidence classifications as a key design requirement for production systems. Any result with a confidence score below a defined threshold should be flagged and routed directly to a human reviewer rather than proceeding through the automated path; 0.85 is a reasonable starting threshold. This approach handles the ambiguous cases that do not fit neatly into a category.


That threshold is a configurable parameter rather than a fixed rule. The appropriate value depends on the risk tolerance of the team and the accuracy observed during initial deployment.


## Step 3: Extract key fields for structured context


Classification identifies the request type. Extraction identifies the information an investigator needs before acting.


A second AI call, using the same Jinba-connected model, pulls structured data from the email body. The prompt instructs the model to return a JSON object containing:


Extract the following fields from the email. If a field is not present, return null.


Fields: customer_name, customer_id, request_type, deadline, case_reference, involved_parties


Email:
{email_body}


Respond only with valid JSON.


This entity extraction step replaces the manual context-gathering that compliance teams identify as the primary time cost in their current process. The investigator who receives the routed task already has the structured summary: who the request concerns, what is being asked, and when a response is due. Investigators move directly to judgment rather than reconstructing context from a raw email thread.


The extracted fields also become the inputs for the logging step in Step 4.


## Step 4: Route to the right team and log every decision


Based on the category returned in Step 2, the workflow routes the request to the appropriate queue or owner. A straightforward routing map covers most compliance inboxes:


- **KYC Request** -> Onboarding team queue
- Regulatory Notice -> Legal and compliance team lead
- Internal Escalation -> Senior investigator
- **Low-confidence classification** -> Manual review queue


Routing creates a task in the relevant system, drafts a summary for the assigned owner, or both. No external reply is sent automatically. The human reviewer receives the routed task with the extracted context attached and decides what response, if any, to send. The human-in-the-loop boundary is that the workflow handles sorting and preparation while the investigator handles judgment and communication.


Every triage event is written to a Google Sheet using Jinba's[Google Sheets tool](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/productivity/google_sheets) . Each row captures:


Field


Value


Timestamp


ISO 8601 datetime of receipt


Sender


Email address


Subject


Original subject line


Category


AI classification result


Confidence


Score returned by the model


Customer Name


Extracted field


Deadline


Extracted field


Case Reference


Extracted field


Assigned To


Routed queue or owner


Review Status


Pending / Approved / Escalated


This log is the audit trail. It records what the system decided, with what confidence, and who it assigned the task to. Regulators and internal auditors can reconstruct every triage decision from this record. Teams that rely on manual inbox management have no equivalent log: decisions happen in someone's head and are not recoverable.


## Technical safeguards for a compliance-grade deployment


Three technical considerations apply when deploying this workflow against a production compliance mailbox.


**Reply loop prevention.** If the shared mailbox receives automated replies from other systems, the workflow can trigger on those replies and classify a machine-generated message. An` X-Auto-Response-Suppress: All` header check at the trigger step filters out those messages before classification.


**API rate limits.** The Microsoft Graph API enforces a limit of 10,000 requests per 10 minutes per application at the service level. For high-volume inboxes, batching multiple read operations into a single Graph request reduces call volume and keeps the workflow within these limits. This is documented in[Microsoft Graph's throttling guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/throttling) .


**Outlook Mail automation and data residency.** Organizations with strict data residency requirements can configure the Jinba workflow so that all processing, including AI inference, remains within their own tenant. The Jinba Outlook Mail tool connects through Microsoft Graph under the organization's own credentials, meaning email content does not pass through a third-party intermediary. This Outlook Mail automation architecture satisfies the data boundary requirements that apply to many regulated entities.


## What to build next


This four-step workflow handles the triage function: sorting, classifying, extracting, and routing. It does not handle response drafting, case escalation logic, or SLA monitoring. Those are reasonable next extensions once the triage layer is stable and producing a clean audit log.


Compliance teams should start by mapping the categories that appear in their compliance inbox. Most compliance inboxes have three to five recurring request types that account for the majority of volume. The classification prompt should be built around those specific categories rather than generic labels. The workflow should run in observation mode first, where it classifies and logs but does not route; confidence scores and classifications should be reviewed against actual emails for two to four weeks. That review period establishes the accuracy baseline and identifies the edge cases that require a dedicated handling rule before routing is enabled.


Jinba's Outlook Mail tool, combined with its Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Sheets integrations, provides the connective layer for this workflow without requiring custom infrastructure. The compliance judgment stays with the team, and the workflow handles the sorting.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is an AI-powered compliance email triage workflow?


An AI-powered compliance email triage workflow automatically sorts incoming compliance-related emails by classifying intent, extracting key fields, routing each message to the right team, and logging every decision. It replaces the manual reading and context-gathering that typically consume analyst time before any real compliance judgment begins.


### How does Jinba automate compliance email triage in Outlook?


Jinba connects to a shared Outlook mailbox through the Microsoft Graph API and runs a scheduled workflow that lists new messages with` OUTLOOK_LIST_MESSAGES` . It then uses Azure OpenAI or Anthropic to classify each message and extract key details, routes the request based on that classification, and logs the outcome to a Google Sheet case tracker.


### What are the four steps in a compliance email triage workflow?


The four steps are list, classify, extract, and route. A scheduled run lists new emails from the mailbox, an AI model classifies each one, key fields are extracted, and the request is assigned to the appropriate team or queue and logged.


### What categories should I use for compliance email classification?


Organizations should start with the recurring request types already present in their compliance inbox. Common categories include KYC Request, Regulatory Notice, Internal Escalation, and General Inquiry, but the classification prompt should be mapped to the three to five categories that account for most of the volume.


### How do you handle low-confidence AI classifications in compliance triage?


Low-confidence classifications should be routed directly to a human reviewer instead of proceeding through the automated path. A confidence threshold such as 0.85 is a reasonable starting point, but the exact value should be treated as a configurable parameter based on team risk tolerance and observed accuracy.


### Does the Jinba compliance triage workflow send automatic replies to customers?


No. The workflow does not send any external email without human approval. It sorts, classifies, extracts, routes, and logs. The investigator who receives the routed task makes the judgment call and decides what response, if any, to send.


### How is compliance triage data logged and audited?


Every triage event is written to a Google Sheet using Jinba's Google Sheets tool. Each row records the timestamp, sender, subject, category, confidence score, extracted fields, assigned owner, and review status, creating a defensible audit trail that regulators and internal auditors can reconstruct.


### What technical safeguards are needed for compliance-grade email automation?


Three key safeguards are reply loop prevention, API rate limit management, and data residency control. Filter out machine-generated replies, batch Microsoft Graph requests to stay within throttling limits, and configure the workflow so email content and AI inference remain within the organization's own tenant.


### How long should you run compliance email triage in observation mode before going live?


Organizations should run the workflow in observation mode for two to four weeks. During this period, the workflow classifies and logs but does not route, allowing teams to compare AI classifications against actual emails, establish an accuracy baseline, and identify edge cases before routing is enabled.
